source_text: Si penitus sensus ejus interpretemur, non aliud dicendum erit secundum matrimonium, quam species stupri. Cum enim dicat, maritos hoc in sollicitudine habere, quemadmodum sibi placeant; non utique de moribus (nam bonam sollicitudinem non sugillaret); et de cultu, et ornatu, et omni studio formae, ad illecebras movendas sollicitos intelligi velit; de forma autem et cultu placere carnalis concupiscentiae ingenium sit, quae etiam stupri caussa est: ecquid videtur tibi stupri adfine esse secundum matrimonium, quoniam ea in illo deprehendo quae stupro competunt? Ipse Dominus: Qui viderit, inquit, mulierem ad concupiscendum, jam stupravit eam in corde suo. Qui autem eam ad ducendum viderit, minus an plus fecit? Quid, si etiam duxerit? quod non faceret. nisi et ad ducendum concupisset, et ad concupiscendum vidisset. Nisi si potest duci uxor, quam non videris nec concupieris. Multum sane interest, maritus an caelebs aliam concupiscat. Omnis mulier etiam caelibi alia est, quamdiu aliena; nec per aliud tamen fit marita, nisi per quod et adultera. Leges videntur matrimonii et stupri differentiam facere per diversitatem illiciti, non per conditionem rei ipsius. Alioquin quae res et viris et foeminis omnibus adest ad matrimonium et stuprum? commixtio carnis scilicet, cujus concupiscentiam Dominus stupro adaequavit. Ergo, inquis. jam et primas, id est, unas nuptias destruis. Nec immerito, quoniam et ipsae ex eo constant, quo et stuprum. Ideo optimum est homini mulierem non attingere, et ideo virginis principalis sanctitas, quia caret stupri adfinitate. Et cum haec etiam de primis et unis nuptiis praetendi ad caussam continentiae possint, quanto magis secundo matrimonio recusando praejudicabunt! Gratus esto, si semel tibi indulsit Deus nubere; gratus autem eris, si iterum indulsisse illum tibi nescias. Caeterum, abuteris indulgentia, cum sine modestia uteris. Modestia a modo intelligitur. Non tibi sufficit de summo illo immaculatae virginitatis gradu in secundum recidisse nubendo; sed in tertium adhuc devolveris, et in quartum, et fortassis in plures, postquam in secunda statione continens non fuisti: quia nec prohibere plures nuptias voluit, qui de secundis provocandis retractavit. Nubamus igitur quotidie, et nubentes ab ultimo die deprehendamur tanquam Sodoma et Gomorra: quo die, Vae illud super praegnantes \[adimplebitur\], id est, super maritos et incontinentes: de nuptiis enim uteri, et ubera, et infantes. Et quando finis nubendi? Credo post finem vivendi.
pass_a_gloss: If we thoroughly interpret its sense, nothing else will be said about a second marriage, except that it is a kind of fornication. For when it says that husbands have this concern, how they may please themselves, it is not certainly about morals, for it would not disparage good concern. And about cultivation, and adornment, and every study of form, it wants to be understood that they are concerned with moving to enticements. But to please by form and cultivation is the nature of carnal concupiscence, which is also the cause of fornication. Does it seem to you that a second marriage is akin to fornication, since I detect in it the things that pertain to fornication? The Lord himself says, 'He who looks at a woman to lust after her has already fornicated with her in his heart.' He who looks at her to marry, has he done less or more? What if he also marries her? Which he would not do, unless he had also lusted after her and looked at her to lust after her. Unless a wife can be married whom you have not seen or lusted after. It makes a great difference, whether a married man or a celibate lusts after another woman. Every woman is another woman to a celibate, as long as she is someone else's, and yet she does not become a wife through anything else, except through what also makes her an adulteress. The laws seem to make a distinction between marriage and fornication through the diversity of what is unlawful, not through the condition of the thing itself. Otherwise, what thing is present for both men and women in marriage and fornication? Certainly the commingling of flesh, whose concupiscence the Lord has equated with fornication. Therefore, you say, now you also destroy first marriages, that is, single marriages. And not undeservedly, since they also consist of what fornication consists of. Therefore, it is best for a man not to touch a woman, and therefore the principal sanctity of a virgin, because it lacks the kinship of fornication. And since these things can also be adduced about first and single marriages as a cause for continence, how much more will they prejudice a second marriage! Be grateful if God has allowed you to marry once; you will be grateful if you do not know that he has allowed you to marry again. Moreover, you abuse indulgence when you use it without modesty. Modesty is understood from measure. It is not enough for you to have fallen from the highest degree of immaculate virginity to a second marriage; but you roll back to a third, and to a fourth, and perhaps to more, after you were not continent in the second station, because he who restrained from provoking second marriages did not want to prohibit multiple marriages. Therefore, let us marry every day, and let us be caught on the last day, like Sodom and Gomorrah, on which day, 'Woe to those who are pregnant,' that is, to husbands and incontinent people, will be fulfilled, concerning the pregnancies of marriages, and breasts, and infants. And when is the end of marrying? I believe it is after the end of living.

pass_b_english: If we press the logic to its core, a second marriage turns out to be nothing but a species of fornication. Scripture says husbands are anxious about how to please themselves (1 Cor 7:33) — not about character, since the text would never disparage a good anxiety; it means they fuss over grooming, adornment, and every effort to enhance their looks in order to arouse desire. But pleasing through appearance and polish is the very signature of carnal lust, which is also the engine of fornication. So does a second marriage strike you as kin to fornication? I catch in it the very marks of fornication. The Lord himself says: "Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matt 5:28). The man who looks at her intending to marry her — has he done less, or more? What if he actually marries her? He would never have done so unless he had first lusted after her and looked with that intent. Unless, of course, a man can marry a woman he has never seen or desired. There is a vast difference between a married man and a celibate lusting after another woman. To a celibate, every woman is 'another woman' as long as she belongs to someone else; yet she becomes a wife only through the very act that would also make her an adulteress. The law tries to separate marriage from fornication by labeling one licit and the other illicit, not by any difference in the thing itself. Otherwise, what single reality is common to both marriage and fornication for men and women alike? The mingling of flesh — and the Lord has equated the lust for that mingling with fornication. "So you're wiping out first marriages too," you object. Not undeservedly, since they are built from the same stuff as fornication. That is why "it is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman" (1 Cor 7:1), and why the virgin's preeminent holiness consists precisely in lacking any kinship with fornication. If these arguments hold even for a first and only marriage as a motive for continence, how much more do they condemn a second! Be grateful if God indulged you once to marry; you will be grateful if you never learn that he indulged you a second time. You abuse the indulgence when you use it without measure; modesty is defined by measure. It wasn't enough for you to fall from the summit of spotless virginity into a second marriage; you roll on to a third, a fourth, perhaps more — because you failed continence at the second stage, and the One who refused to legislate second marriages did not want to forbid multiple ones either. So let us marry every day, and be caught on the Last Day like Sodom and Gomorrah — the day when "Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing infants" (Matt 24:19; Luke 21:23) will be fulfilled, that is, over husbands and the incontinent: for marriage means wombs, breasts, and babies. When does the marrying stop? I suspect only when life itself ends.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B provides necessary scripture citations (1 Cor 7:33, Matt 5:28, 1 Cor 7:1, Matt 24:19, Luke 21:23) which are required for the allusions/quotes in the Latin (e.g., 'Qui viderit...', 'Optimum est homini...', 'Vae illud super praegnantes'). Pass A is a faithful literal gloss. Both preserve the nuances of agency and modality.

The Latin text is correctly identified as Tertullian's 'On Exhortation to Chastity 9'. The translation preserves the original meaning, including the use of 'second marriage' for 'secundum matrimonium' and 'the kinship of fornication' for 'stupri adfinitate'. The passage is fully translated without omissions, and the scriptural citations match the quoted text. The title 'Chastity and Marriage' accurately reflects the content of the passage.
